topic: DGX Spark has 128 GB and a 70B still crawls at 2.7 tokens/s
title: DGX Spark speed math: bandwidth beats gigabytes
description: Everyone reads 128 GB as 'runs anything'. A measured 2.7 tokens per second says otherwise. You'll learn the one division that predicts chat speed on a DGX Spark, and why a bigger model can be the faster one. Subscribe for daily local-AI shorts. (Narration is AI-generated.)
hook_text: Your Spark isn't slow. Doorway's narrow.
hook_candidates: You load the biggest model that fits. It answers like a fax machine.
Your Spark isn't slow. Its doorway is narrow.
This 120B model outruns a 70B on the same desk.
Eight hundred three tokens in. Two point seven out.
You unbox the Spark, feed it a 70B, and wait. And wait.
The model isn't dumb. The road it walks is narrow.
Seventy or one-twenty billion? One division decides.
LMSYS benchmarked a 70B on the Spark. The decode crawled.
The model that fits is not the model that talks.
You bought 128 gigabytes. Your chatbot still types two words a second.
narration_full: Your Spark isn't slow, its doorway is narrow. L M S Y S measured two point seven tokens a second from a seventy-billion-parameter model on one. You ordered the Spark for a hundred twenty-eight gigabytes of unified memory, or the order page is still open. The plan writes itself: load the biggest model that fits, expect chat speed. Everyone's math says fitting is the whole game. Same box, same model, two speeds. It reads your prompt at eight hundred three tokens a second. It writes the answer at two point seven, slower than your group chat types. Why the gap. Reading is one wide pass of math, and the Spark's compute eats it. Writing is one token at a time, and each token re-reads the model's weights from memory. The compute barely works during decode. The memory does the hauling. Picture a kitchen where the chef chops instantly and every ingredient fits through one narrow door. The chef is the compute. The door is the memory bus: two hundred seventy-three gigabytes a second. For reading your prompt, one wide delivery, the picture breaks. So the speed ceiling is one division. Bandwidth divided by the gigabytes each token re-reads. A dense seventy-billion model in eight-bit re-reads about seventy gigabytes per token. The ceiling sits under four tokens a second. Two point seven is that ceiling with overhead. What a token re-reads is the active weights, the slice the model actually uses. Quantize to four-bit and each token carries half the bytes. You give up a little accuracy, and casual chat never notices. Or a mixture of experts, a model that wakes only a few specialists per word. G P T O S S one twenty B is bigger on paper and chats comfortably. The spec sheet did not lie. It printed the doorway's width in smaller type. A model that does not fit does not run. And those hundred twenty-eight gigabytes are why a two-hundred-billion-parameter model loads on a desk at all. Capacity picks what loads. Bandwidth picks how it talks. Before you download a model for this box, find the gigabytes it re-reads per token. Divide two hundred seventy-three by it. That one number tells you the chat speed before the download starts.
